bridge: B01 introduced the DOM and text insertion. The examples belong only in the named training environment.
teaching:
### Follow the input to the page

A reflected input returns in the immediate response. A stored input is saved and later displayed. A DOM-based issue can arise when browser-side code reads data and inserts it into an unsafe page operation. These describe different paths to the same important question: can supplied content become executable?

### Match the output handling to its context

Text placed in HTML, an attribute, a URL or JavaScript is interpreted under different rules. Use the framework's appropriate safe output mechanism for the actual context. Setting text content is different from asking the browser to parse a string as HTML.

If a feature deliberately accepts HTML, use a well-maintained sanitiser configured for the allowed markup. Sanitising means removing or transforming content outside that policy; it is not the same as escaping plain text.

### Understand the possible impact

A script executing in a page's origin can often read or act on information available to that page. Cookie attributes can protect particular cookie access, but they do not make arbitrary script execution harmless.

### Use additional protections sensibly

A suitable Content Security Policy can reduce some script execution paths and provide useful restrictions. It supplements correct data handling rather than replacing it. Trace source, transformations and final insertion point when testing the fix.
example: Local B01 page: input value: practice Safe sink: result.textContent = value Expected DOM: literal text, no child b element Stored variant: save the same text as a note; reload and render with textContent. The storage step changes persistence, not the safe insertion rule.
explanation: The marker is markup-shaped text, not an attack script. It lets you distinguish literal insertion from HTML parsing. A note stored safely in the database can still become dangerous if a later view inserts it into an executable context.
exercise: Open your local B01 greeting file, enter practice and click Greet. Right-click the output and choose Inspect (or the browser’s equivalent); the result paragraph should contain text and no nested b element. If comfortable using the developer-tools Console on this file, type document.querySelector("#result").childElementCount and expect 0. For a persistence demonstration with no database setup, save the exact marker in a separate plain-text practice-note.txt file, close it, reopen it, paste its contents back into the input and greet again. This models stored data being rendered later; it does not implement a real reflected or stored web endpoint. Explain which step persisted data and which step decided how it was displayed.
solution: Both displays show literal angle brackets and have zero child elements inside the result paragraph. The greeting may include “Hello, ” before the marker; that is still text. Saving and reopening practice-note.txt preserves the value, while textContent controls its interpretation on each display. Reflected XSS involves an immediate response path; stored XSS involves a persisted value later reaching an unsafe rendering path. The local marker demonstrates the parsing distinction without executing an attack script.
challenge: An app safely renders a note in its main view but builds an inline script from the same note in an export preview. Explain why the first repair does not prove the preview safe and propose a design avoiding the script context.
challenge_solution: Each sink needs independent context analysis. Keep data out of inline executable source, pass it through a structured data channel and render plain text with DOM text APIs. Test both views with harmless delimiter/markup-shaped inputs.
